content: Direct current (DC) refers to the unidirectional flow of electric charge. It is generated by sources such as batteries, thermocouples, solar cells, and commutator-type electric machines like dynamos. While DC typically flows through conductors like wires, it can also pass through semiconductors, insulators, or even a vacuum, as seen in electron or ion beams. Unlike alternating current (AC), where the direction of charge flow alternates periodically, DC maintains a constant direction of flow. Historically, DC was also referred to as galvanic current. DC can be derived from an AC supply using a rectifier, a device that allows current to flow in only one direction. Rectifiers typically use electronic components, though historically, electromechanical elements were also employed. Conversely, DC can be converted back into AC using an inverter or a motor-generator set. The first commercial electric power transmission system, developed by Thomas Edison in the late 19th century, utilized DC. However, due to the advantages of AC in power transformation and long-distance transmission, modern electric power distribution systems predominantly use AC. For applications requiring DC, such as third-rail power systems, AC is distributed to substations, where rectifiers convert it into DC. DC is widely used to charge batteries and serves as the primary power supply in nearly all electronic systems. Large quantities of DC power are essential in industrial processes like aluminum production and other electrochemical applications. DC is also employed in certain railway propulsion systems, particularly in urban areas. High-voltage DC (HVDC) is used to transmit significant amounts of power over long distances from remote generation sites or to interconnect AC power grids. In electrical engineering, the term DC refers to power systems that operate with a single polarity of voltage or current. It also describes the constant or slowly varying local mean value of voltage or current. For instance, the voltage across a DC voltage source remains constant, as does the current through a DC current source. The DC solution of an electric circuit is the state where all voltages and currents are constant. Any stationary voltage or current waveform can be decomposed into a DC component (the average value over time) and a time-varying component with zero mean. Although DC stands for Direct Current, it can also refer to constant polarity. In this context, DC voltages may vary over time, such as the raw output of a rectifier or the fluctuating voice signal on a telephone line. Some forms of DC, like those produced by voltage regulators, exhibit minimal voltage variation but may still show fluctuations in output power and current. DC installations often use specialized sockets, switches, and fixtures, primarily due to the low voltages involved, which differ from those used for AC systems. It is crucial not to reverse polarity in DC appliances unless the device includes a diode bridge to correct for this, as most battery-powered devices do not. DC is commonly found in low-voltage applications, especially those powered by batteries or solar power systems, as both produce only DC. Most automotive systems use DC, even though the alternator generates AC, which is then rectified to produce DC. Similarly, most electronic circuits require a DC power supply. Fuel cells, which generate electricity by combining hydrogen and oxygen with a catalyst, produce only DC. Many telephones connect via a twisted pair of wires, separating the AC component (audio signal) from the DC component (used to power the phone). Telephone exchange equipment, such as DSLAMs, typically uses a standard -48V DC power supply. The negative polarity is achieved by grounding the positive terminal of the power supply system and battery bank, a measure taken to prevent electrolytic deposition. Electrified third rails are used to power both underground (subway) and overground trains, providing a reliable source of DC power for railway systems.
